newsitem.title: MEXICO: FOCUS - Repsol becoming Latam gas giant.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Repsol becoming Latam gas giant.

text.p: Spain's Repsol bolstered its Latin American presence on Thursday, edging out five competitors for the coveted natural gas concession in Mexico's industrial center of Toluca.

The company plans investments of about $30 million in the Mexican state over the next five years. In that time, it pledged to transport the fuel to 47,279 residential clients at a cost of 47 U.S. cents per gigacalorie.
Toluca adds to Repsol's presence in Mexico in the recently granted natural gas concession in northern industrial city Saltillo. It is also expected to win a contract for border city Nuevo Laredo.
"Toluca is our third win in the past six weeks, after Bogota and Rio de Janiero," Repsol's director general in Mexico Alfonso Martinez told reporters.
Repsol bought a 53 percent stake in Bogota's gas distributor for $148 million last month and last week won the privatization of Rio de Janiero state gas company CEG.
The Spanish powerhouse is not content with its inroads so far in Mexico. It next has its eyes on the prized Mexico City tender, expected to be awarded later in the year.
Repsol has bounced back after losing the first two Mexican concessions it bid for, in Mexicali and Chihuahua.

Its bid in Toluca included a price to consumers 10 percent lower than its nearest competitor. The Energy Regulatory Commission (CRE) chooses the winning bid among the lowest costs offered to clients and the most residential clients the bidders pledge to serve.
"In the Mexicali bidding we offered ten times the winning client price. After almost a year we have learned our lesson," Martinez said.

The Toluca site was particularly coveted not only because of its large industrial presence and natural gas consumption, but because of the low cost of hooking up clients who are bunched close together.

"In Toluca we have high consumption levels combined with a more dense concentration of industry than in other regions," CRE president Hector Olea said, explaining the lower natural gas transportation charge to clients in the region.
Repsol estimates that by its fifth year of distribution in Toluca, natural gas consumption will be about 25 billion cubic meters per year, of which 22.5 billion will be for industry.
Repsol also has the option of taking a minority stake in a new 369-mile (595-km) pipeline, worth about $40 million, that will need to be built to bring natural gas to the Toluca area.
The new pipeline will complement an existing one owned by state gas monopoly Petroleos Mexicanos (Pemex) that is already at full capacity.
Some losing bids offered a greater client base than Repsol but higher prices to customers.
The consortium between U.S. Noram Energy Corp and Mexico's Gutsa Construcciones offered the second lowest bid of 64 U.S. cents per gigacalorie.

Other bidders were France's Gaz de France and Mexico's Mexigas; Mexico's Centra Gas de Toluca, Canadian WestCoast and U.S. Coastal Gas Toluca; Mexico's Consortium Sistema Automatico de Gas and Toluca Disco Holding and U.S. Enova Corp ; and Mexico's Grupo Mexicano de Desarollo, Canada's B.C. Gas International and U.S. Shell Oil Company.
Repsol's Martinez also said the company would be interested in other investments in Mexico's oil and gas industry.
"There are now new possibilities opening in secondary petrochemicals. Things are still unknown, so we can't know if we will participate or not," Martinez added.
Along with natural gas, secondary petrochemicals are slated to be opened for private investment. Other oil interests are sole property of Pemex.
